items_missed: Never got or used the customer's name — not once in 8.5 minutes
Never asked how the customer was doing; the customer asked him ('Yeah, how are you today?') and he answered without returning it
Never confirmed Einstein actually has availability on Wednesday the 16th — he confirmed the customer's requested date but never said the date was open
Never captured the destination address, yet applied an out-of-zone travel fee to 'both of the locations'
Never asked about boxes at all — the single biggest time driver on any move went unprobed on a partial-move job
Customer volunteered that another bed 'gonna get moved later on but it can't go now' — a second-trip / additional-stop signal that was never explored
No probe on additional rooms, special considerations (long walk, narrow halls, tight turns), packing needs, storage, access/parking/HOA, or destination stairs
Never asked the moving-stressors question
Quoted the trip fee as '$100' and then corrected it to '$175' with no acknowledgment of the change
Never stated the number of movers or trucks — the customer bought a $190/hr rate without ever learning what crew size that buys
No typical time range given for the job; he substituted the assertion 'I don't believe this job is gonna go over that' twice instead of a range
No No Worries Damage Coverage mention — and he told the customer there are 'no insurance fees,' which leaves coverage worse than unexplained
Meet Your Mover never mentioned
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned
Disassembly/reassembly never mentioned despite a king mattress and an adjustable mechanical bed frame on the list
Never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens
No sense-check anywhere in the pricing or clock explanation, on a call where the customer explicitly said he could not follow
Entire Save Your Ass prep speech skipped
No email handoff — never told the customer a written quote or confirmation email was coming; gave a verbal phone number instead
No close attempt — customer said 'I'm still looking around so I'll give you a call probably tomorrow' and the reply was 'Alrighty, no problem sir'
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?'
No hours given (direct number only)
Customer explicitly complained about pace: 'you're talking way fast and I can[not] understand you sir'
Said 'good afternoon' on a call placed at 8:51 PM CT
One 'Yes ma'am' slip on a male customer
top_strength: Two things genuinely worked. First, the opener is the closest thing in this run to a real agenda statement — 'Do you have like a 15[-]20 minutes to discuss all the details so I can [work] you up an estimate,' which named a timeframe, named the sequence (details first, then estimate), and got an explicit 'Sure, I do. Yes sir' before he proceeded. Second, his recovery under direct criticism was excellent: when the customer said he was talking too fast, Cameron said 'I apologize' with no defensiveness, slowed down, and then re-stated the travel fee three separate times while the customer found paper and wrote it down, never once showing impatience. He also read the customer's unspoken worry correctly at the end — the 'you guys are so far away' concern got a clean, reassuring 'We do have a branch in Tampa... we're about 25 minutes from that first location.' The partial-move probe was real work too, pinning down one mattress versus two and correctly identifying the adjustable base as a heavy item.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix is pace and comprehension-checking, because the customer told him outright: 'you're talking way fast and I can[not] understand you sir.' Everything downstream of that broke — the customer ended up doing the arithmetic himself out loud, twice, and got it wrong before Cameron corrected him. The fix is one sentence, used three times per call: 'Does that make sense so far?' after the rate, after the minimum, and after the fee. On this call specifically, the numbers should have been delivered as one clean total with a pause: 'So at the two-and-a-half hour minimum that's $475, plus the $175 travel fee, brings you to $650 flat. Does that make sense?' Second priority is that this call has no written trail and no crew size. He never told the customer how many movers $190 an hour buys, and he never offered an email — he read out his cell number instead, so the customer's only record of this quote is what he wrote on a sheet of paper. Say it every time: 'I'm going to send you a confirmation email with all of this in bold at the top — give it a look and just reply if anything's off.' Third, he had the perfect close handed to him: he mentioned no deposit and no cancellation fee immediately AFTER the customer said he was still shopping, when it should have come one beat earlier as the reason to book — 'no deposit and no cancellation fee, so let me lock the 16th in and you can keep shopping with zero risk.' LIVE BUSINESS RISKS, and these matter more than the 28: (1) he quoted the trip fee as $100 and then as $175 on the same recorded call, and the customer wrote down $175 — that discrepancy needs to match EMMA before anything goes out. (2) He told the customer there are 'no additional taxes or insurance fees,' never mentioned No Worries Damage Coverage or the 60c/lb baseline, and never corrected the impression — the customer can reasonably have heard either 'insurance is included' or 'there is no insurance,' and both are wrong. (3) He promised twice that the job likely will not exceed the 2.5-hour minimum on a move with roughly 34 miles between addresses, a king mattress and a mechanical base, and zero information about boxes — that is an unforced estimate-accuracy risk and a bad move-day conversation waiting to happen. (4) He applied an out-of-zone travel fee to 'both of the locations' without ever capturing the destination address. (5) Cross-branch exposure: a San Antonio manager quoted a Tampa move with no email, no confirmation, and only his own 210 number given to the customer — there is no evidence this lead exists anywhere the Tampa branch can see it.
phone_presence_notes: Patient and respectful under a direct complaint — apologized instantly and re-explained the fee three times without irritation, and the customer ended warm ('thanks so much Cameron, I appreciate it') — but he never used the customer's name, never returned the how-are-you, and leaned on a near-verbatim 'Yes sir' for most of his turns, which reads more transactional than warm.
audio_review_reason: The customer explicitly said the rep was talking too fast to be understood, which is precisely the dimension a transcript cannot measure. Listen to this one before the coaching conversation — it is the clearest pace-and-clarity example available and worth using as a training clip alongside the recovery, which was genuinely good.
